hints: Picture the familiar shapes of s (sphere) and p (dumbbell) orbitals, then recall that most d orbitals have one extra feature with four lobes.
walkthrough:
Recall what a d orbital looks like**
Think of building up: an s orbital is a sphere, a p orbital is two lobes. A d orbital is the next step up in complexity. Four of the five d orbitals look like a four leaf clover, four equal lobes meeting at the nucleus. The fifth one, $\text{d}_{z^2}$, looks different with two lobes along z plus a doughnut ring around the middle.

Draw one cleanly**
Pick the easiest one, for example $\text{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ with four lobes pointing along the x and y axes, or $\text{d}_{xy}$ with lobes between the axes. Label the axes if you can. Keep lobes symmetrical and meeting at the centre. That alone earns the mark.

Final answer: Draw any one correct 3d orbital: four lobes in a cloverleaf for $\text{d}_{xy}$, $\text{d}_{xz}$, $\text{d}_{yz}$ or $\text{d}_{x^2-y^2}$, or two lobes plus central torus for $\text{d}_{z^2}$, with correct orientation on axes.

hints: Start from atomic number of Ni (28) and remember that 4s fills before 3d in the atom, but 4s electrons are lost first when forming ions.
walkthrough:
Build the Ni atom**
Ni has 28 electrons. Fill up to argon core $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^6$ which accounts for 18, leaving 10. Those go as $3\text{d}^84\text{s}^2$, because 4s fills before 3d is complete.

Form Ni3+ by removing outer electrons first**
A common slip is to remove from 3d first. Always remove $4\text{s}$ electrons before $3\text{d}$. For $3+$ you remove the two $4\text{s}$ electrons plus one $3\text{d}$ electron: $3\text{d}^84\text{s}^2$ becomes $3\text{d}^7$ with no $4\text{s}$ electrons left.
Final answer: Ni: $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^63\text{d}^84\text{s}^2$ ; $\text{Ni}^{3+}$: $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^63\text{d}^7$

hints: Start from the middle box with five degenerate orbitals, then recall that ligands split them into two sets with opposite patterns for octahedral and tetrahedral.
walkthrough:
Start from degeneracy**
With no ligands, all five 3d orbitals repel electrons equally, so they sit at exactly the same energy. That is what degenerate means.

Split with ligands**
When ligands approach, some d orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised more. In octahedral, two orbitals point at ligands so you get 3 low, 2 high with a large gap. In tetrahedral, no orbitals point directly, the pattern flips to 2 low, 3 high and the gap is much smaller, about half the octahedral gap.

Final answer: Isolated ion: five degenerate d orbitals at same energy. Octahedral: split into lower set of three ($\text{t}_{2\text{g}}$) and upper set of two ($\text{e}_{\text{g}}$) with large gap. Tetrahedral: split into lower set of two ($\text{e}$) and upper set of three ($\text{t}_2$) with smaller gap.

hints: Link the splitting you just drew to light: what must happen for an electron to move between the lower and upper d sets?
Think about which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has photons with energy matching typical d orbital gaps.
walkthrough:
Create the gap for light to match**
Splitting produces a small energy difference between d sets. That gap happens to correspond to photon energies in the visible part of the spectrum.

Absorb and promote**
When white light shines through, a photon of exactly the gap energy is absorbed. Its energy is used to excite an electron from the lower d level to the upper d level. Because some wavelengths are removed, the light that gets through looks coloured.

Final answer: Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels with gap in visible region. A photon of visible light is absorbed, promoting an electron from the lower d set to the upper d set (d-d transition). The colour seen is the complementary colour transmitted.

hints: Compare the two complexes: same metal and oxidation state, but different ligands ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$ vs $\text{NH}_3$), so focus on what ligands change.
walkthrough:
Spot the only change**
Both are Cu(II) octahedral complexes, only the ligand changes from $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to $\text{NH}_3$. Different ligands repel d electrons differently and create a different $\Delta E$.

Link gap to colour**
A different gap needs a different photon energy $E = hf$ to promote the electron. So different wavelengths are absorbed and different colours are transmitted, pale blue vs deep purple-blue.
Final answer: Different ligands cause a different size of d orbital splitting ($\Delta$), so a different frequency / wavelength of visible light is absorbed.

hints: Look at where the absorption peaks are on the wavelength axis and where absorption is lowest.
Remember the solution colour is what is NOT absorbed, the light that passes through to your eye.
walkthrough:
Read the spectrum**
The y axis is absorption. There is a tall peak over blue around 400 nm and a second peak over red around 600 nm. In the middle, around 480 to 500 nm labelled green, the curve dips to a minimum.

Flip absorption to observed colour**
Do not say it looks blue because it absorbs blue. It is the opposite. Blue and red are removed from white light, green passes through almost untouched, so your eye sees green.

Final answer: colour of solution: green
explanation: solution absorbs most strongly in blue (approx 400 nm) and red (approx 600 nm) regions and absorbs least in green, so green light is transmitted.

hints: Keep V in the centre with six octahedral positions, place four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and two $\text{Cl}$ in each diagram.
For one isomer put the two identical $\text{Cl}$ ligands opposite each other (180 degrees), for the other put them next to each other (90 degrees).
walkthrough:
Draw trans-[V(H2O)4Cl2]+**
Put V in the centre. Put the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands on the vertical axis, one up one down, so the $\text{Cl}$-V-$\text{Cl}$ angle is 180 degrees. Fill the four equatorial positions with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ using wedge, hatched and solid bonds to show 3D.

Draw cis-[V(H2O)4Cl2]+**
Now move one $\text{Cl}$ to be next to the other, so the $\text{Cl}$-V-$\text{Cl}$ angle is 90 degrees. The four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands fill the other four octahedral sites. These two arrangements cannot be superimposed by rotation.

Final answer: Isomer 1 (trans): octahedral V with two $\text{Cl}$ opposite each other, four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in plane. Isomer 2 (cis): octahedral V with two $\text{Cl}$ adjacent at 90 degrees, four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ occupying remaining sites.

hints: Recall the name for isomerism in square planar and octahedral complexes caused by different spatial positions of the same ligands.
walkthrough:
Name the spatial isomerism**
The formula is identical, only the 3D positions of $\text{Cl}$ differ, cis (adjacent) vs trans (opposite). This is geometrical isomerism, also called cis-trans isomerism.
Final answer: cis-trans / geometrical isomerism

hints: Remember each en ($\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) is bidentate and must occupy two adjacent octahedral sites, forming a chelate ring.
Think of three propeller blades around V: the two mirror forms twist in opposite directions and cannot be superimposed.
walkthrough:
Place three chelate rings**
Each en uses its two N atoms to grab V at 90 degrees, shown as an N-N arc. With three en ligands all six octahedral sites are filled. Draw the arcs spanning cis positions, not trans.

Create the mirror pair**
Arrange the three arcs like a propeller twisting one way for isomer 1, then draw the exact mirror image twisting the opposite way for isomer 2. Check they are non-superimposable, just like left and right hands. Those are the pair of enantiomers.

Final answer: Two non-superimposable mirror image structures of octahedral $[\text{V}(en)_3]^{3+}$, each with three bidentate en ligands forming chelate rings, one left-handed propeller ($\Lambda$) and one right-handed propeller ($\Delta$).

hints: Recall the term for non-superimposable mirror image isomers that rotate plane polarised light.
walkthrough:
Identify chirality**
The complex has no plane of symmetry and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images. This is optical isomerism, the two forms are enantiomers.

hints: Write Kstab for $[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, remembering which species are omitted.
walkthrough:
Apply the equilibrium law**
For ligand exchange, $K_{\text{stab}}$ is the equilibrium constant for formation of the complex from the aqua ion. Put complex concentration on top, aqua ion times ligand concentration to the power of 6 below. Omit water as pure liquid: $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6^{2+}]}{[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^6}$$ Note the power 6 matches the six $\text{NH}_3$ ligands.

hints: Compare the magnitudes $4.8 \times 10^7$ vs $2.0 \times 10^{18}$ and think which equilibrium lies much further to the right.
walkthrough:
Let the numbers decide**
Both ligands compete for the same $\text{Ni}^{2+}$. The $K_{\text{stab}}$ for $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ is about $10^{11}$ times larger. The equilibrium forming the en complex lies far further to the right, so even with equal moles of ligands, the chelated complex dominates.

Final answer: $[\text{Ni}(en)_3]^{2+}$ is produced in larger amount because its $K_{\text{stab}}$ is much greater ($2.0 \times 10^{18}$ >> $4.8 \times 10^7$), so it is much more stable due to chelate effect.

hints: Treat en as bidentate occupying cis sites only, then consider the two monodentate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands as either trans (opposite) or cis (adjacent).
Ask whether the cis-$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ arrangement is chiral and can exist as a non-superimposable mirror pair, unlike the trans form.
walkthrough:
Find cis and trans forms**
With two bidentate en ligands, four sites are taken by N atoms. The two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can be opposite each other to give trans-$[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(en)_2]^{2+}$, or next to each other at 90 degrees to give cis-$[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(en)_2]^{2+}$. That is cis-trans (geometrical) isomerism.

Split the cis form into two**
The trans form has symmetry and is achiral, only one version. The cis form has no mirror plane, it is chiral like a propeller. It exists as two non-superimposable mirror images, a pair of optical isomers. So total stereoisomers = 1 trans + 2 cis enantiomers = 3.

Final answer: Three stereoisomers in total: one trans-$[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(en)_2]^{2+}$ with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ opposite each other, and a pair of enantiomers for cis-$[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2(en)_2]^{2+}$ with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ adjacent, which is chiral and shows optical isomerism in addition to cis-trans isomerism.
